```{r setup, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library("DT") # Interactive HTML tables
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
```

Here we describe the the data and the results of the regional [2nd order __sensu__ Johnson [-@johnson_comparison_1980]] assessment of reindeer selection for grazing sites in the Malå reindeer herding community, Sweden, under the presence of mining and wind power development, for the three snow-free seasons: calving, summer, and autumn. We also refer to this analysis as a large-scale assessment of habitat selection. We describe:

- the reindeer GPS data used for the analyses;
- how the analysis was set up: 
- the results of the habitat selection analysis (HSA).

# Goals of the analysis

The main question driving the HSA analyses is: how is the selection of grazing sites by reindeer across seasons affected by wind power, mining, and other human infrastructure and activity, at a large (regional) scale? In other words, how does reindeer selects for habitat at a 2nd order selection [sensu @johnson_comparison_1980]?

The specific questions are:

-   Are there cumulative impacts of multiple disturbance of the same type, e.g. multiple turbines or multiple wind parks? In other words, is there evidence of the impact of the density of wind turbines instead of only the nearest wind turibine?
-   Are there cumulative impacts of different types of disturbance, e.g. both wind power and mining?
-   What is the zone of influence of the impacts, i.e. up to which distance from disturbance is reindeer behavior altered?
-   How does the impacts change across seasons - calving, summer, and autumn?

# Methods

## Data

```{r load_data, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
load("../../data/01_GPS/05_annotated_data/data_annotated_calving_ready_2h_rsf.RData")
load("../../data/01_GPS/05_annotated_data/data_annotated_summer_ready_2h_rsf.RData")
load("../../data/01_GPS/05_annotated_data/data_annotated_autumn_ready_2h_rsf.RData")

# calving
summ_calving_year <- data_ready_calving_rsf_2h |> 
  dplyr::filter(case_ == TRUE) |> 
  dplyr::group_by(year) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(n = n(),
                   n_ind = length(unique(id)))

summ_calving <- apply(summ_calving_year, 2, sum)

# summer
summ_summer_year <- data_ready_summer_rsf_2h |> 
  dplyr::filter(case_ == TRUE) |> 
  dplyr::group_by(year) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(n = n(),
                   n_ind = length(unique(id)))

summ_summer <- apply(summ_summer_year, 2, sum)

# autumn
summ_autumn_year <- data_ready_autumn_rsf_2h |> 
  dplyr::group_by(year) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(n = n(),
                   n_ind = length(unique(id)))

summ_autumn <- apply(summ_autumn_year, 2, sum)
```

GPS data was collected by Sami reindeer herders through GPS collaring female reindeer between 2008 and 2018. No data was collected between 2012 and 2014, the years that followed the construction of the wind farm. Data was collected with a 2 hour fix rate, and failures or gaps were not considered for the analyses, and used to define the separation of the movement tracks into bursts. Data was only included in the analysis if there was at least forty consecutive days of movement data for each individual. Data was manually checked for all reindeer-years so that all positions representing reindeer being herd or GPS position of collars not attached to animals were removed. Furthermore, we used Bjørneraas et al (2010) procedure to remove spikes and outliers, and removed all locations found within known fenced areas and corrals, which are typically used for reindeer handling.

The HSA was based on data of `{r} summ_calving[3]` reindeer tracked during calving, `{r} summ_summer[3]` reindeer tracked during summer, and `{r} summ_autumn[3]` reindeer tracked during autumn. Table C1 shows the number of individuals and number of used GPS positions recorded in each year. 

```{r data_summary_year, echo=FALSE}
#| label: data_summary_year
#| fig-cap: "Table C1. Number of reindeer monitored (number of GPS positions recorded) in each year and season."
#| 
summ_data <- summ_calving_year |>
  dplyr::mutate(Phase = c(rep("Before construction", 2),
                          rep("Construction", 2),
                          rep("Operation", 4)),
                .after = 1) |> 
  dplyr::rename(`n - calving` = n,
                `number individuals - calving` = n_ind) |> 
  dplyr::left_join(
    summ_summer_year |> 
      dplyr::rename(`n - summer` = n,
                `number individuals - summer` = n_ind),
    by = "year"
  ) |> 
  dplyr::left_join(
    summ_autumn_year |> 
      dplyr::rename(`n - autumn` = n,
                `number individuals - autumn` = n_ind),
    by = "year"
  ) |> 
  dplyr::rename(Year = year) |> 
  dplyr::relocate(starts_with("number"), .after = "Phase")

summ_data |> 
  dplyr::mutate(Calving = paste0(`number individuals - calving`, " (", `n - calving`, ")"),
                Summer = paste0(`number individuals - summer`, " (", `n - summer`, ")"),
                Autumn = paste0(`number individuals - autumn`, " (", `n - autumn`, ")")) |> 
  dplyr::select(Year, Phase, Calving, Summer, Autumn) |> 
  DT::datatable()
```

## Statistical modeling

We modeled habitat selection using binomial regression following [@fieberg_how_2021]. Used GPS positions were compared to available positions spread randomly throughout the availability area within each season. The area available was different across seasons (see Figs AXXX in Appendix A) and it was defined by the reindeer herding community borders on the North, West, and South, and the fence **HOW TO CALL THIS FENCE?** in the East during calving. In summer and autumn the animals often crossed the fence, so the eastern limits of the availability area were defined by a buffer around the used positions, accounting for the reindeer herding community borders and the main roads. More details on the availability areas are presented in Appendix A. 

We ran models using use/availability as a response variable and the effects of wind power, mining, and other infrastructure (private and public roads, power lines, houses, trails) as covariates. We also added other land cover and phenology related variables - elevation, slope, aspect, terrain position index (TPI), and date of the start of the season (SOS) (or end of season, EOS, for autumn). TPI is a measure of variation in the relief of a neighborhood, computed by comparing the elevation of a site with the average elevation on the neighborhood, for a given neighborhood size/scale [@de_reu_application_2013]. Here the TPI was computed using neighborhoods of different sizes (150 m, 250 m, and 510 m) and the best TPI scale was defined through model selection (see below). SOS and EOS are phenological variables based on NDVI that show the time of peak greening and browning of the vegetation in spring and autumn [@kong_phenofit_2022]. Given our questions, our focus was mainly on estimating the impacts of wind power and mining, so the other variables were mainly included to control for their possible, additive effects. All variables that were not in log scale were standardized to mean 0 and variance 1, to facilitate convergence of the model fits.

We assessed if and how the impacts of wind power and mining accumulated using the approach from Niebuhr et al. [-@niebuhr_estimating_2023]. To represent the spatial influence of wind power and mining, we computed zones of influence (ZOI) that decayed exponentially from the disturbance source and vanished at varying distances, from 100 m to 10 km (100 m, 250 m, 500 m, 1 km, 2.5 km, 5 km, 10 km). For wind power, we computed both the (exponentially weighted) density of wind turbines, which accounts for the cumulative influence of multiple nearby wind turbines and wind farms, and the ZOI of the nearest feature, which just accounts for the distance decay influence of a single, nearest feature. For mining we only considered the ZOI of the nearest mine, since there is only one main mining site in the study area. For simplicity, the influence of all other infrastructure types was modeled using the log-distance to the nearest feature, i.e. their ZOI was not directly evaluated. We built binomial regression models using each possible combination of ZOI radii and type (cumulative vs. nearest) for wind power and different ZOI radii for mining, together with different scales for the TPI and an additive effect of all the other variables. To evaluate the impact of wind turbines, we used a before-after set up, comparing the selection for the ZOI of wind turbines across construction phases - before construction, during construction, and operation.

The overall model structure we fitted was the following:

```{r}
base_formula <- case_ ~ 
  # habitat selection
  scale(dem) + I(scale(dem)^2) + scale(slope) + cos_aspect + 
  scale(sos) + 
  log(power_lines_dist+1) + log(priv_road_dist+1) + log(public_road_dist+1) + 
  log(trails_dist+1) + 
  log(house_dist+1) + 
  # mining habitat selection
  scale(mining_Krist_nearestXXX) +
  # wind habitat selection
  wf_name + 
  landcover*phase*scale(wind_turbines_ZZZ) +
  # tpi habitat selection
  tpi_scale_TTT
```

where `case_` is our response variable, `dem` is elevation, `phase` is the temporal phase of the wind farms (before construction, during construction, operation), and `wf_name` is the name of the wind farm closest to each point, and `wf_name` refers to the name of the closest wind farm to each point, added as a fixed effect to control for differential effects close to the Åmliden wind park, which lies along a large fenced area. The model includes the logarithm of the distance to the nearest infrastructure for power lines, roads, trails, and houses, the ZOI (exponential distance-decay) of the mine, and an interaction bewteen land cover, phase, and the ZOI of wind turbines (considering either the density or the nearest infrastructure only).


The terms `XXX`, `ZZZ`, and `TTT` in the model structure above represent scales or variables that varied across models fitted. To evaluate the most likely ZOI for the mine and the wind turbines, whether there was a cumulative impact of multiple wind farms, and at which scale the TPI most affected reindeer habitat selection and movement, we replaced these variables in the model structure above using each possible combination of ZOI radii and type (cumulative vs. nearest) for wind power and the different ZOI radii for mining, together with different scales for the TPI. Models were compared through the Akaike information criterion (AIC), and the most parsimonious model was selected as the one with smaller AIC [@burnham_model_2002].

To interpret the results, we first checked the structure of the best ranking models (through the AIC and their difference; we considered models different if $\Delta AIC$ > 2; Burnham and Anderson 2002) and compared how they differed qualitatively. Second, we evaluated the coefficients of the best ranked model for each season. Third, for habitat selection, we plotted the relative selection strength [RSS; @avgar_relative_2017] for wind turbines and land cover, as well as for mining, using the function `ggpredict()` from the package `ggeffects`. Fourth, we made spatial predictions of the best ranked model to visualize and quantify how much the predicted habitat suitability changed before, during, and after the construction of the wind farms, for each season. Finally, we used these models to compute the proportional differences in habitat suitability in the construction and operation phases, compared to the habitat suitability for reindeer before the wind farms construction. These maps are the ones that more clearly show the ZOI of the mine and the wind farms, the cumulative impact of different types of infrastructure, and possibly the cumulative impact of multiple wind farms, if present.

## Model selection

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# calving
load("../../output/rsf_calving_multi_zoi_table_landcover_grouped.rda")
tab_models_calving <- tab_models[-1,]
form_calving <- tab_models_calving$definition[1] |> 
  gsub(pattern = "\n   ", replacement = "")
# summer
load("../../output/rsf_summer_multi_zoi_table_landcover_grouped.rda")
tab_models_summer <- tab_models[-1,]
form_summer <- tab_models_summer$definition[1] |> 
  gsub(pattern = "\n   ", replacement = "")
# autumn
load("../../output/rsf_results/rsf_autumn_multi_zoi_table_lc_grouped.rda")

```

Summary of best ranked models:

-   **Calving. Impact of the nearest wind turbine, ZOI radius = 5 km; ZOI of the mine with radius 10 km:** \
    `{r} paste(form_calving)`

-   **Summer. Cumulative impact of wind turbines, ZOI radius = 10 km; ZOI of the mine with radius 10 km:**\
    `{r} paste(form_summer)`

-   **Autumn. Impact of the nearest wind turbine, ZOI radius = 10 km; ZOI of the mine with radius 10 km:** \
    `{r} paste(form_autumn)`

### Calving

Table B2 shows the ranking of most parsimonious models for 2nd order habitat selection
during calving. The best model for calving included the additive effect of mining at 10 km radius and 
of the zone of influence of the nearest wind turbine at 5 km radius (Table B2). 
The second, third, and forth ranking models also included ZOI of the nearest wind turbine
at large scales, which does not include any support to the hypothesis of cumulative impacts of multiple 
wind turbines or parks during calving. All the best ranking models support a large ZOI radius for both the mine (10 km) and the wind turbines (5-10 km).

```{r aic_calving, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
#| label: aic_calving
#| fig-cap: "Table B2. Table of model selection for the HSA models for calving. Columns are zone of influence (ZOI) radius for mining and wind turbines, scale for the terrain position index (TPI), AIC of the model, dAIC of each model in relation to the most parsimonious model, and the formula with each model's structure. Variables with 'Log' correspond to the log-distance to the nearest feature for that variable."

aic_calving <- readr::read_csv("../../output/rsf_results/rsf_calving_AIC_table_complete.csv")

aic_calving |> 
  dplyr::slice(-1) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(dAIC = round(dAIC - dAIC[1], digits = 2),
                aic = round(aic, digits = 2),
                tpi = sub("tpi_cat_s", "", tpi)) |> 
  dplyr::relocate(definition, .after = last_col()) |> 
  dplyr::select(-lc) |>
  dplyr::rename(`Mining ZOI radius` = 1,
                `Wind turbine ZOI radius` = 2,
                TPI = tpi,
                AIC = aic,
                formula = definition) |> 
  DT::datatable()
```

### Summer

Table B3 shows the ranking of most parsimonious models for 2nd order habitat selection 
during summer. The best model for summer included the additive effect of mining at 10km radius and 
of the density of wind turbines at 10 km radius (Table B3). This means there was evidence
of cumulative impacts of multiple wind farms on reindeer habitat selection at regional scale
on summer.
All the best ranking models support a large ZOI radius for both the mine (5 - 10 km) and 
the wind turbines (5-10 km).

## Disturbance effects on habitat selection

Here we present the coefficients of the HSA models. Even though all results come
from the same models, we split the way we present the parts of the resulting model, to ease
its interpretation. In this section we restrict ourselves on
presenting the coefficients of all infrastructure and landscape covariates, without going into 
details regarding the impact of wind farms on habitat selection. 
These results are shown in details in the following sections.

### Coefficients for other infrastructure - All seasons

Here we show the coefficient estimates for all the infrastructure types, excluding wind turbines which present interactions in the model
structure and are explored further down. The estimates are put together for the different seasons in table B5
so it is easy to compare the effects between them.

A summary of the results:

- The mine strongly avoided in all seasons, especially during calving, with a large ZOI radius of 10 km;
- Public roads were avoided in all seasons;
- Private roads and trails were avoided during calving and summer, but were selected in autumn;
- Power lines were avoided only during calving and were selected in the other seasons.
- Houses were avoided during autumn, but were select during calving and summer (*why??*)
- Areas with a later start of season and a later end of season timing were selected during calving and autumn, respectively; in contrast, areas with an earlier start of seasons were selected during summer.

```{r coef_general, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
#| label: coef_general
#| fig-cap: "Table B5. Coefficient estimates for the infrastructure types and the start/end of season for all three seasons."
#| 
# read calving
coef_calving <- readr::read_csv("../../output/rsf_results/rsf_calving_coef_table_landcover_grouped.csv") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(significant = as.factor(if_else(p.value < 0.05, 1, 0)),
                p = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", round(p.value, 3)),
                select = case_when(
                  (estimate > 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate < 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "avoidance/negative",
                  (estimate < 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate > 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "selection/positive",
                  TRUE ~ "no effect"
                ))

# read summer
coef_summer <- readr::read_csv("../../output/rsf_results/rsf_summer_coef_table_log_lc_grouped.csv") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(significant = as.factor(if_else(p.value < 0.05, 1, 0)),
                p = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", round(p.value, 3)),
                select = case_when(
                  (estimate > 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate < 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "avoidance/negative",
                  (estimate < 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate > 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "selection/positive",
                  TRUE ~ "no effect"
                ))

# read autumn
coef_autumn <- readr::read_csv("../../output/rsf_results/rsf_autumn_coef_table_log_lc_grouped.csv") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(significant = as.factor(if_else(p.value < 0.05, 1, 0)),
                p = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", round(p.value, 3)),
                select = case_when(
                  (estimate > 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate < 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "avoidance/negative",
                  (estimate < 0 & grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) | (estimate > 0 & !grepl("log", term) & significant == 1) ~ "selection/positive",
                  TRUE ~ "no effect"
                ))

coef_all <- dplyr::tibble(season = c(rep("calving", nrow(coef_calving)), 
                          rep("summer", nrow(coef_summer)),
                          rep("autumn", nrow(coef_autumn)))) |> 
  cbind(
    dplyr::bind_rows(coef_calving, coef_summer, coef_autumn)) |> 
  dplyr::filter(grepl("log|nearest|sos|eos", term)) |> 
  dplyr::filter(!grepl("wind", term)) |> 
  dplyr::select(-c(statistic, significant, p.value)) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(term)

coef_all |> 
  DT::datatable()
```

## Impacts of mining and wind turbine on step selection

Here we plot, for each season, the effect of the mine and the wind turbines, while
keeping all the other variables at their median values, to illustrate the mean
effect of these two types of infrastructure.

### Calving

The mine in Kristeneberget was strongly avoided during calving, according to the HSA (Fig. B1), with a ZOI radius of 10 km.

![Figure B1. Relative probability of use of areas as a function of the distance to the mine in Kristineberget in calving. Areas close to the mine are avoided up to ca. 10 km.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_calving_mining.png)

The effect of the wind turbines before, during, and after the construction of the wind farms, for different land use types, is shown in Fig. B2. 

Open lands (which include clear cuts), coniferous forests, and mires were avoided up to 2.5-5 km from the wind turbines, when we compare the reindeer behavior before and during/after the construction of the turbines. Deciduous forests (including forested wetlands) in the proximity 
of the wind parks were also avoided during construction phase, but not during operation phase.

![Figure B2. Relative probability of use of areas as a function of the distance to the nearest wind turbine in calving, using Ytterberg wind park as a reference.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_calving_wind_phase_landcc_groupedytteberg.png)

The effect is qualitatively similar when reindeer are closer to each of the four wind parks, but is smaller when close to Åmliden wind park in the Southeast, most probably because of joint effect of the fence which is a barrier for reindeer movement. This differential behavior is shown in the spatial prediction of the habitat suitability for reindeer in calving (and also in the other seasons) in Fig. B3.

![Figure B3. Predicted habitat suitability for reindeer in calving before the construction of the wind farms (left), during the construction (center), and during operation of the wind farms (right). The top row shows the habitat suitability, in a gradient from 0 (white) to 1 (green), and shows the location of the wind turbines and the mine. It also highlights a buffer of 5 km around the wind farms and 10 km around the mine, just as a reference for interpretation. The bottom row shows the GPS data for each phase superimposed over the habitat suitabiltiy predictions.](FB3_HSA_suitability_calving.png)

Fig. B3 shows the habitat suitability predicted from the best ranked models for all phases, as well as the reindeer GPS positions in each of the phases. The models fit well the GPS data and show very strong avoidance of the area around the mine, represented by a large areas in white with very small habitat suitability. It also shows avoidance of the wind turbines during construction and operation phases, even though this difference is more evident when looking at the difference in habitat suitability (see Fig. 3 in the main text).  

**WE STILL NEED to compute the proportion in habitat suitability lost within the ZOI, just as a reference to be reported!!!**

### Summer

As during calving, the mine in Kristeneberget was strongly avoided during summer, with a ZOI radius of 10 km (Fig. B4).

![Figure B4. Relative probability of use of areas as a function of the distance to the mine in Kristineberget in summer. Areas close to the mine are avoided up to ca. 10 km.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_summer_mining.png)

During summer, there was evidence of cumulative impacts of multiple wind farms on reindeer habitat selection at regional scale. To interpret, however, it is necessary to account for the density of wind turbines within a neighborhood. In Fig. B5 we show the predicted response curves against the distance to the wind farm in it was composed by n = 1 turbine (top row) or by n = 10 wind turbines (bottom row). The difference between predictions shows the cumulative dimension of the density of wind turbines.

As we expected, reindeer did not avoid wind turbines during summer. Reindeer already used the mountains where the turbines were built before, most probably because the are open areas with wind that is suitable for releasing the pressure of insect harassment [@skarin_insect_2004; @valente_attacked_2020]. Reindeer seem to have increased the use of these mountains after the construction of the turbines, also. (**why?**) 

![Figure B5. Relative probability of use of areas versus the distance to the nearest wind turbine in summer, using Ytterberg wind park as a reference. Top row shows the (hypothetical) prediction if the wind park was composed only by n = 1 wind turbine - a small impact. The bottom row shows a cumulative impact of n = 10 wind turbines, which gets much larger.](../../output/rsf_results/summer_wind_phase_landcc_ytte_dist.png)

Fig. B6 shows the habitat suitability predicted from the best ranked models for all phases, as well as the reindeer GPS positions in each of the phases. The models fit well the GPS data and show high selection for the mountains where the wind farms were built in all phases, including during and after the construction of the wind turbines.

![Figure B6. Predicted habitat suitability for reindeer in summer before the construction of the wind farms (left), during the construction (center), and during operation of the wind farms (right). The top row shows the habitat suitability, in a gradient from 0 (white) to 1 (green), and shows the location of the wind turbines and the mine. It also highlights a buffer of 5 km around the wind farms and 10 km around the mine, just as a reference for interpretation. The bottom row shows the GPS data for each phase superimposed over the habitat suitabiltiy predictions.](FB4_HSA_suitability_summer.png)

### Autumn

As during calving and summer, the mine in Kristeneberget was strongly avoided during autumn, with a ZOI radius of 10 km (Fig. B7).

![Figure B7. Relative probability of use of areas as a function of the distance to the mine in Kristineberget in autumn. Areas close to the mine are avoided up to ca. 10 km.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_autumn_mining.png)

In the proximity of the wind farms, deciduous forests and mires were avoided more strongly in the construction and operation phases, compared to the baseline (before construction; Fig. B8). The difference in selection between areas close to the wind farms and far from wind farms was also higher in the period preconstruction than during construction and operation phases, which points to an overall decrease in habitat suitability in the surroundings of the wind farms. 

![Figure B8. Relative probability of use of areas as a function of the distance to the nearest wind turbine in autumn, using Ytterberg wind park as a reference.](../../output/rsf_results/rsf_autumn_wind_phase_landcc_grouped_ytteberg.png)

Fig. B9 shows the predicted habitat suitability in the three different phases and the GPS data showing reindeer positions in autumn. The avoidance of wind turbines and decrease in habitat suitability is more pronounced and evident during the operation of the wind farms (Fig. B9), what illustrates the large ZOI radius
found also during autumn. There was no evidence of cumulative impacts of multiple wind farms, though, as the best ranked models included the impact of the nearest wind turbine only.

![Figure B9. Predicted habitat suitability for reindeer in autumn before the construction of the wind farms (left), during the construction (center), and during operation of the wind farms (right). The top row shows the habitat suitability, in a gradient from 0 (white) to 1 (green), and shows the location of the wind turbines and the mine. It also highlights a buffer of 5 km around the wind farms and 10 km around the mine, just as a reference for interpretation. The bottom row shows the GPS data for each phase superimposed over the habitat suitabiltiy predictions.](FB5_HSA_suitability_autumn.png)
